blocks.text: K. considered whether he ought not to make a hasty departure now; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect of his being able to do so during the sermon, he would then have to remain as long as it lasted, he was losing so much time at the office, he had long since ceased to be obliged to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was 11. But could a sermon really be preached? Could K. alone constitute the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who only wanted to view the church? At bottom he was nothing else either. It was absurd to think that a sermon was to be preached, now at 11 o'clock, on a weekday in the most dreadful weather. The priest—a priest it undoubtedly was, a young man with a smooth, dark face—was evidently going up only to extinguish the lamp, which had been lit by mistake.

It was not so, however; rather, the priest examined the light and turned it up a little higher, then he turned slowly toward the balustrade, which he grasped along the angular front edge with both hands. Thus he stood for a while and gazed around without moving his head. K. had retreated a considerable distance and was leaning with his elbows on the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw somewhere, without precisely fixing the spot, the verger with bent back crouching peacefully as though after a finished task. What a stillness now reigned in the cathedral! But K. had to disturb it, he had no intention of remaining here; if it was the priest's duty to preach at a fixed hour regardless of circumstances, then let him do so, it would succeed even without K.'s assistance, just as K.'s presence would certainly not heighten the effect. Slowly, therefore, K. set himself in motion, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, then entered the broad central aisle and walked there too quite undisturbed, save that the stone floor rang out beneath the lightest step and the vaults echoed it faintly, yet unceasingly, in a manifold, regular progression. K. felt a little forsaken as he walked alone there between the empty pews, perhaps observed by the priest; moreover, the size of the cathedral seemed to him to lie just at the limit of what is still endurable for human beings. When he reached his former place, he fairly snatched without further delay at the album left lying there and took it with him. He had almost left the area of the pews and was approaching the open space that lay between them and the exit when he heard the priest's voice for the first time. A powerful, practiced voice. How it pierced the cathedral, ready to receive it! Yet it was not the congregation that the priest was addressing, it was unmistakable and there was no evasion, he called: Josef K.!

K. stopped short and looked down at the floor before him. For the moment he was still free, he could still walk on and make off through one of the three small dark wooden doors that were not far ahead of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that he had indeed understood, yet did not choose to concern himself with it. If, however, he turned around, he was caught, for then he had made the confession that he had understood well, that he truly was the one called, and that he also meant to obey. Had the priest called out once more, K. would certainly have gone away, but since all remained quiet, however long K. waited, he did turn his head a little, for he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood calmly in the pulpit as before, yet it was clearly to be seen that he had noticed the turn of K.'s head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not now turned around completely. He did so and was beckoned nearer by the priest with a wave of his finger. Since everything could now be done openly, he ran—he did so also out of curiosity and to cut the matter short—with long, flying strides toward the pulpit. At the first pews he halted, but to the priest the distance still seemed too great; he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply lowered forefinger to a spot right in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed in this too; in that spot he already had to tilt his head far back in order still to see the priest. “You are Josef K.,” said the priest, and raised one hand on the balustrade in an indefinite gesture. “Yes,” said K.; he thought of how openly he had always given his name in the past, for some time now it had been a burden to him, moreover people with whom he was meeting for the first time now knew his name; how pleasant it was to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. “You are accused,” said the priest in a particularly low voice. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed of it.” “Then you are the one I am looking for,” said the priest. “I am the prison chaplain.” “Ah, I see,” said K. “I had you summoned here,” said the priest, “to speak with you.” “I did not know it,” said K. “I came here to show an Italian the cathedral.” “Leave aside what is incidental,” said the priest. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?” “No,” answered K., “it is an album of the city's sights.” “Lay it down,” said the priest. K. threw it away so violently that it flew open and slid a distance across the floor with crumpled pages. “Do you know that your trial is going badly?” asked the priest. “It seems so to me as well,” said K. “I have taken every possible trouble, but so far without success. To be sure, I have not yet finished the petition.” “How do you imagine the end?” asked the priest. “Formerly I thought it must end well,” said K., “now I sometimes doubt it myself. I do not know how it will end. Do you know?” “No,” said the priest, “but I fear it will end badly. You are held to be guilty. Your trial will perhaps not even get beyond a lower court. At least for the present, your guilt is held to be proven.” “But I am not guilty,” said K. “It is a mistake. How can a human being be guilty at all? Here we are all human beings, one like another.” “That is true,” said the priest, “but that is how the guilty are accustomed to speak.” “Do you too have a prejudice against me?” asked K. “I have no prejudice against you,” said the priest. “I thank you,” said K. “All the others, however, who are involved in the proceedings have a prejudice against me. They instill it in those uninvolved as well. My position is becoming ever more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the priest. “The verdict does not come all at once; the proceedings gradually pass over into the verdict.” “So that is how it is,” said K., and lowered his head. “What do you intend to do next in your case?” asked the priest. “I mean to seek more help,” said K., and raised his head to see how the priest judged it. “There are still certain possibilities that I have not made use of.” “You seek too much outside help,” said the priest disapprovingly, “and especially from women. Do you not see that it is not the true help?” “Sometimes, and indeed often, I could agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could induce a few women whom I know to work together for me, I would have to prevail. Especially with this court, which consists almost exclusively of womanizers. Show the examining magistrate a woman from a distance and, merely to get there in time, he will overrun the court table and the accused.” The priest inclined his head toward the balustrade; only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to weigh him down. What sort of storm might there be outside? That was no longer a gloomy day, that was already deep night. No stained glass of the great windows was capable of breaking the dark wall with even a single gleam. And at this very moment the verger began to extinguish the candles on the main altar one after another. “Are you angry with me?” K. asked the priest. “Perhaps you do not know what sort of court you serve.” He received no answer. “After all, they are only my experiences,” said K. Up above it still remained silent. “I did not mean to offend you,” said K. Then the priest shouted down to K.: “Can you not see two steps ahead?” It was shouted in anger, yet at the same time like someone who sees another falling and, because he himself is startled, cries out heedlessly without meaning to.
